title: Slow conversion when loading from CSV and saving as Parquet
body: I am loading several large datasets containing 20GB or more of CSV data and want to export them to Parquet. On DuckDB 0.7.1, loading a gzip-compressed CSV into a local on-disk database takes about three minutes, but copying the resulting all-VARCHAR table to Parquet takes upwards of three hours. I am using the DuckDB CLI on an Apple Silicon M1 iMac with 16GB RAM, a 1TB SSD, and macOS Ventura 13.2.1. Is there a better approach than creating the table with read_csv_auto(..., all_varchar=true) and then copying it to Parquet?

symptoms_visible: On DuckDB 0.7.1, loading the gzip CSV into an on-disk all-VARCHAR table takes about three minutes, while writing that table to Parquet takes upwards of three hours.
N0.label: N0 very slow Parquet export reported

symptoms_visible: On the newer development build, a direct gzip-CSV-to-Parquet conversion finishes in about 550 seconds instead of three hours.
The direct conversion takes about the same time with insertion-order preservation enabled or disabled.
N1.label: N1 newer build and direct conversion tested

symptoms_visible: With the experimental parallel CSV reader, the gzip conversion finishes in about 32 seconds, but the resulting Parquet file contains only 30,559,373 rows instead of 212,363,079.
N2.label: N2 experimental gzip parallelism truncates input

symptoms_visible: Parallel reading of the uncompressed CSV produces all 212,363,079 rows, while every tested compressed-input run using the experimental parallel reader produces a much smaller, incomplete file.

Decompressing the source separately takes about 1 minute 9 seconds and the uncompressed CSV can then be processed in roughly 2 to 3 minutes; letting this build read the gzip source is much slower unless the unsafe experimental path is used.
N3.label: N3 compressed parallel-reader defect isolated

symptoms_visible: After updating to a build with the newer parallel CSV reader, all of the input files appear to load successfully.
Trying to read the generated Parquet file fails with 'No magic bytes found at end of file'.
N4_x.label: N4_x newer parallel reader produces unreadable Parquet

symptoms_visible: On the latest source build, the compressed CSV converts to a readable Parquet file in about 2 minutes 57 seconds.
The resulting Parquet file opens successfully and contains all 212,363,079 rows.
N_terminal.label: terminal fast and complete conversion verified

question_patterns: Could you retry the conversion with a current development build and report the elapsed time?
Can you test a direct COPY from the compressed CSV to Parquet on the latest build?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested v0.7.2-dev1322. A direct COPY from ccaed182.csv.gz to ZSTD Parquet took 549.536 seconds.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The current development build still takes about three hours for the same direct conversion.
The direct conversion takes about ten minutes rather than 549.536 seconds.

question_patterns: Can you compare the same direct conversion with insertion-order preservation enabled and disabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The direct run took 549.536 seconds normally and 551.849 seconds after I set preserve_insertion_order=false. Both outputs were 4,794,409,184 bytes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Disabling insertion-order preservation reduces the direct conversion from about nine minutes to under one minute.

solution.intent: Move off DuckDB 0.7.1 to a current build containing the recent VARCHAR-to-Parquet performance work, avoid the intermediate persistent table, and use a direct SELECT-node COPY so CSV options such as all_varchar can be supplied.
solution.concrete_example: Use a current build and run COPY (SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto('ccaed182.csv.gz', all_varchar=true)) TO 'ccaed182.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET, CODEC ZSTD), rather than first materializing a persistent table.

edges.comment: Messages c4 and c8-c19, all on the reporter's M1 iMac: a maintainer points to the recent VARCHAR Parquet performance improvement and direct conversion; the reporter installs dev1322, records raw timings, and confirms the SELECT-node syntax needed for all_varchar.

question_patterns: Could you enable the experimental parallel CSV reader for a test run and report the raw timing and output checks?
Please run the direct conversion with parallel CSV reading in a throwaway session and check the resulting row count.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With experimental_parallel_csv=true and preserve_insertion_order=false, the direct all-VARCHAR conversion completed in 31.687 seconds.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The parallel test takes about nine minutes and produces the same output as the serial run.
The parallel test completes in 35 seconds instead of 31.687 seconds.

question_patterns: How many rows are in the Parquet output from that test, compared with the source?
Can you count the rows with the parallel reader enabled and disabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The parallel run produced only 30,559,373 rows. Reading the same gzip CSV without the experimental parallel reader produces 212,363,079 rows.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both runs produce the full 212,363,079 rows and the Parquet files read successfully.

edges.comment: Messages c10-c21 on the reporter's system: the maintainer requests the experimental parallel-reader probe. The reporter supplies raw elapsed times and row counts; the conclusion that compressed parallel reading is defective is not placed in the measurement answer.

question_patterns: Does the same behavior occur if the CSV is decompressed first?
Can you compare compressed and uncompressed input with the same settings?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The uncompressed CSV works as expected with parallel reading. It converts in 168.212 seconds, and the Parquet output contains all 212,363,079 rows.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The uncompressed CSV is truncated to the same 30,559,373 rows.

question_patterns: What do you see across the combinations of compressed input, direct versus SELECT-node COPY, order preservation, and parallel reading?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I benchmarked all 16 combinations. Every compressed-input case with experimental_parallel_csv=true produced a much smaller, incomplete output file; the corresponding non-parallel compressed runs produced full-size files.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The failures follow SELECT-node COPY regardless of compression or parallelism.
The same compressed parallel cases are incomplete, with slightly different output sizes and timings.

question_patterns: How does separate decompression followed by conversion compare with reading the gzip file directly?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: gzip decompresses the source to disk in 1 minute 9 seconds. DuckDB then processes the uncompressed file in about 2:07 to 2:59, while the best direct gzip times without the broken experimental path are around 11:31 to 19:10.

edges.comment: Messages c23 and c26-c32, all produced by the reporter: the reporter voluntarily runs a 16-case benchmark matrix and isolates the observable failure to compressed inputs using the experimental parallel reader.

solution.intent: Update to a build containing the rewritten parallel CSV reader so compressed CSV input is handled by the supported parallel path rather than the older experimental implementation.
solution.concrete_example: Build the latest source after the parallel CSV reader changes land, rerun the compressed and uncompressed cases, and validate each resulting Parquet file rather than relying only on COPY completion.

edges.comment: Messages c33-c40 on the reporter's system: a maintainer says the compressed parallel-reader defect was fixed, and the reporter retests after that work lands. COPY appears successful, but read_parquet reports missing trailing magic bytes, so this update alone is a real, documented failed resolution.

solution.intent: Update to a current source build containing the high-memory/OOM correction for parallel compressed-CSV conversion, retain the one-pass direct COPY workflow, and verify both readability and the complete row count before declaring success.
solution.concrete_example: Build current DuckDB, then run SET preserve_insertion_order=false; COPY (SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto('ccaed182.csv.gz', all_varchar=true)) TO 'ccaed182.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET, CODEC ZSTD). Afterward, open the file with read_parquet and compare COUNT(*) with the source.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers determined from the shared data and debugging that high memory usage in the parallel conversion led to the OOM killer and left Parquet output incomplete, explaining the missing trailing magic bytes. That causal diagnosis is engineer-side inference; the reporter supplied timings, file sizes, row counts, and the raw read_parquet error.

edges.comment: Messages c40-c44 on the reporter's M1 iMac: after maintainers debug the shared files and fix the high-memory/OOM behavior, the reporter compiles v0.7.2-dev2675, completes the conversion in 2:57, opens the Parquet output, and confirms all 212,363,079 rows. The final version and verification are the reporter's own system, not another participant's benchmark.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted cause of the unreadable output: high memory usage in the parallel compressed-CSV conversion could trigger the OOM killer and leave an incomplete Parquet file without trailing magic bytes.

Must connect the original three-hour behavior to the old DuckDB build and use a current build with the VARCHAR-writing and parallel CSV improvements, preferably with a direct SELECT-node COPY rather than an intermediate persistent table.
Must preserve required CSV parsing options such as all_varchar=true in the direct conversion.
Must not recommend the old experimental parallel CSV flag on the development build as a valid fix: with gzip input it read only 30,559,373 of 212,363,079 rows.
Must not treat successful COPY completion after only the first parallel-reader update as resolution, because those generated Parquet files failed with 'No magic bytes found at end of file'.
Must ask the reporter to verify a build containing the memory fix by opening the generated Parquet file and confirming the complete row count before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced independent developer who is comfortable compiling DuckDB from source, writing SQL and Ruby benchmark scripts, inspecting file sizes, timing commands, and validating row counts, but asks for guidance on DuckDB-specific COPY syntax and settings.
persona_hint.communication_style: Highly enthusiastic, cooperative, and unusually thorough; posts exact commands, raw timings, file sizes, screenshots, and benchmark matrices, and promptly validates proposed builds.
